analysis.one_liner: Puts every major federal regulation on an expiration clock unless regulators formally re-approve it under cost-benefit review.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate committee: it received no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have put every major federal rule — any regulation with $100 million or more in annual economic impact — on an automatic termination clock of roughly four to seven years. Unless the agency and the White House regulatory office re-approved the rule after a cost-benefit review, it would simply stop having legal effect, and deadlines that depended on it would freeze. Smaller rules could be targeted by petitions from 'any person adversely affected,' for a $20 fee, with court review if the petition was denied. New major rules would expire after three years unless compliance required heavy capital investment.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses regulated by major federal rules. Rules costing $100 million or more a year would lapse unless affirmatively re-approved, and re-approval would require the agency to re-clear cost-benefit and risk-assessment hurdles. Affected companies could also petition to put smaller rules through the same sunset process for a $20 fee, and sue if the government dragged its feet on deciding. Proponents framed this as weeding out obsolete and duplicative rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Regulated businesses facing major federal rules

how_it_helps.text: Significant rules — those with $100 million or more in annual economic effect — would terminate automatically in four to seven years unless reviewed and continued, forcing agencies to justify every major rule over and over.
New significant rules would expire after three years by default, extended to seven only if the rule came from negotiated rulemaking or required substantial capital investment to comply with.

Any person adversely affected by a smaller rule could petition for a sunset review for a $20 fee, with a decision required within 90 days and court review available if the petition was denied or the government delayed unreasonably.
To survive, a continued rule would have to meet all the legal requirements that would apply to a brand-new rule, including cost-benefit analysis and standardized risk assessment.
Congressional committees could also request sunset reviews of non-significant rules.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who rely on federal health, safety, environmental, and consumer protections. Rules protecting air, water, workplaces, and food would lapse by default unless regulators raced the clock to re-approve them, and the bill allowed only up to a six-month extension in emergencies. Federal agencies would also absorb a permanent, massive review workload. Because the costs of regulation fall on identifiable companies while the benefits — cleaner air, safer products, fewer injuries — are spread across everyone, the sunset structure tilted each review toward the regulated side.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone relying on federal health and safety rules

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith case for the bill is real: some regulations do become obsolete, duplicative, or outdated by changing technology, and a periodic review with public comment could catch those. The bill itself required agencies to weigh whether a rule produced genuine health, safety, or environmental benefits before continuing it.

The cost an honest supporter had to acknowledge: rules protecting diffuse public interests would expire automatically if the review process slipped, and once a rule terminated, any deadlines that depended on it were suspended until a new rule was issued — creating gaps in enforcement and compliance during review.

The bill centralized the decision in one White House office — the Administrator of the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs — which would decide which rules got reviewed first, whether a rule was 'significant,' and whether an agency's recommendation to continue a rule could take effect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Periodic review of regulations is a legitimate idea, and some rules deserve to die. But this design made expiration the default and re-approval the hurdle, with cost-benefit tests that weigh concentrated, measurable compliance costs against diffuse, hard-to-price benefits like avoided illnesses. That asymmetry favors regulated industries in every review. The petition process, judicial review, and the freeze of dependent deadlines add tools and friction that largely serve regulated parties. The bill would have created genuine accountability for agencies, but its default rules and centralization of power in one White House office made it easier for major public protections to lapse than to survive.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee in October 1995, and nothing ever happened to it — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Sen. Spencer Abraham introduced the Regulatory Review Act of 1995 on October 20, 1995, with six other senators joining as original sponsors.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Governmental Affairs.
That was the last action in the record: the bill never received a committee vote or floor action, and it died when the 104th Congress ended.
The bill attracted 8 cosponsors — 7 Republicans and 1 Democrat.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Everyday people simply kept the regulatory status quo: no existing federal rule was put on an expiration clock, and no one lost or gained anything concrete. Regulated industries, which stood to gain a built-in mechanism for challenging and terminating major rules, were denied that tool.

for.name: Sen. Spencer Abraham
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Regulatory Review Act of 1995 and recruited fellow senators to sponsor it.

for.name: 1 of 46 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making the cosponsor list 7 Republicans and 1 Democrat.

against.name: Senate Committee on Governmental Affairs
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on October 20, 1995 and never acted on it — no hearing, markup, or committee vote appears in the record before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Support was nearly all Republican: the sponsor and 7 of 8 cosponsors were Republicans, with one Democrat joining; no floor vote ever occurred, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.industry: Businesses subject to major federal rules (manufacturing, energy, chemicals, finance)
industries.note: Any rule costing $100 million or more annually would expire in three to seven years unless affirmatively re-approved, giving regulated companies repeated chances to press for its termination, and a $20 petition let any affected business force a sunset review of smaller rules. Because compliance costs are concentrated on these firms while the benefits of regulation are spread across the public, the sunset structure favors them in every review.

industries.industry: White House regulatory office (OIRA, Office of Management and Budget)
industries.note: The bill would make the OIRA Administrator the gatekeeper of every major federal rule — designating which rules are 'significant,' setting termination timetables, and able to block an agency's recommendation to continue a rule. That entrenches White House control over regulation, an office historically used to slow or soften new rules.

Banking agencies would have to put their rules through sunset review like everyone else, but the bill carved out their independence: rather than the White House office, each banking agency head would hold the power to approve or reject continuation of its own rules.
